The Arrow darter Etheostoma sagitta is a small-bodied darter endemic to the Cumberland and Tennessee River drainages, where it occupies clear, moderate-gradient headwater streams. Field surveys have documented that individuals at the onset of gonadal development exhibit a standard length of approximately 4.8 centimeters [Lp = approximately 4.8 centimeters], a size threshold that corresponds to the transition from the immature juvenile phase to reproductive capability. This species displays a relatively rapid early growth trajectory, with sexually mature individuals typically measuring between 4.8 and 6.0 centimeters in standard length during their first reproductive season. The maximum ultimate standard length recorded for the Arrow darter reaches 10.44 centimeters [Li = 10.44 centimeters], a value derived from photographic analysis of the largest individuals collected during systematic bioassessment surveys. This asymptotic size is consistent with the modest body plan typical of darters in the subgenus Catonotus, which rarely exceed 12 centimeters in total length even under optimal habitat conditions.

Reproductive investment in the Arrow darter is tightly coupled to the thermal regime of its headwater stream habitats. Under laboratory conditions maintained at 13 °C [T = 13 °C], gravid females produce a maximum of approximately 2.2 eggs per day across the spawning season, which corresponds to an annual fecundity of nearly 800 eggs per female per year [Ri = nearly 800 eggs per female per year] when expressed over a 365-day period. This daily rate of reproductive output was determined from sequential spawning trials conducted under controlled photoperiod and temperature regimes. The eggs themselves are demersal and adhesive, with each fertilized ovum measuring approximately 1.9 millimeters in diameter. Based on the assumption of spherical geometry and a density approximating that of freshwater, the wet weight of a newly fertilized egg is estimated at 0.0036 g [Wwb = 0.0036 g]rams, a value that reflects the modest yolk reserves available to the developing embryo prior to the onset of exogenous feeding.

The thermal environment plays a critical role in shaping the life history schedule of the Arrow darter, particularly the timing of key developmental milestones. At a constant water temperature of 13 °C [T = 13 °C], captive-reared individuals attain sexual maturity approximately 547.5 days after hatching [tp = approximately 547.5 days after hatching], corresponding to roughly 1.5 years of age. This prolonged juvenile period is characteristic of darters inhabiting cool, unproductive headwater streams, where resource availability constrains somatic growth rates. The age at puberty derived from these laboratory observations aligns well with field-based estimates of standard length at maturation of 4.8 centimeters, indicating that the thermal regime is a strong predictor of developmental rate in this species. Comparisons with congeneric species, such as the fringed darter Etheostoma crossopterum, suggest that the Arrow darter occupies an intermediate position along the slow-fast life history continuum.

Adult body size in the Arrow darter exhibits a pronounced allometric relationship with body mass, as described by length-mass regressions derived from preserved museum specimens. The ultimate wet weight for this species, representing the maximum recorded body mass attained by fully mature adults, reaches 12.55 g [Wwi = 12.55 g]rams. This mass corresponds to individuals approaching the asymptotic standard length of 10.44 centimeters and is consistent with the general formula 0.00513 times standard length raised to the power of 3.14, a length-mass relationship that has been validated across multiple populations within the Cumberland Plateau ecoregion. In contrast, the wet weight at birth is several orders of magnitude smaller, with each newly hatched prolarva weighing only 0.0036 g [Wwb = 0.0036 g]rams, reflecting the limited maternal investment per offspring. This stark contrast between neonatal and adult mass underscores the necessity of a prolonged growth phase.

The total lifespan of the Arrow darter, as estimated from mark-recapture studies conducted in undisturbed stream reaches, is approximately 1460 days [am = approximately 1460 days] under natural conditions at ambient water temperatures averaging 13 °C [T = 13 °C]. This corresponds to a maximum longevity of roughly 4 years, a duration that is typical for small-bodied darters in the genus Etheostoma that exhibit iteroparous breeding strategies. Mortality in this species is heavily concentrated during the first year of life, with very few individuals surviving beyond three years owing to predation pressure from larger stream fishes and seasonal environmental extremes. When considered alongside the age at puberty of 547.5 days after hatching [tp = 547.5 days after hatching], this lifespan indicates a life history in which the reproductive window occupies approximately the final two-thirds of an individual's existence, a pattern commonly observed among darters inhabiting cool, stable headwater environments where annual recruitment is low but adult survival is moderately high at a temperature of 13 °C [T = 13 °C].
